title: PR #966: feat(return): explicit eligibility, business-stated deadlines, typed fees
content:
## TL;DR, suggested changes for #634

- **Eligibility is explicit.** `eligibility.type` is `window`, `unlimited`, or `not_accepted`, replacing `final_sale` and an omitted `window`. An omitted `eligibility` means not stated, never unlimited.
- **The business states the deadline, and platforms do no date math.** A window is presentable terms: `duration`, an ISO 8601 duration, plus `anchor`. Once the anchor event has occurred, the business resolves the actual deadline and states it as `expires_at`, an RFC 3339 instant.
- **Fees are one extensible list.** Each entry in `fees[]` is typed by what it is for, uses reverse-domain kinds with vendor extensions, can be scoped to channels, and is priced by its fields: `amount`, `basis_points`, `max_amount`. Fees are estimated maximums. `methods` becomes the set of channels the policy guarantees.

## Example

At checkout, the policy states terms:

```json
{
  "type": "dev.ucp.shopping.policy.return",
  "description": { "plain": "30-day returns from delivery for a refund or exchange. Free returns in store. By mail: $5 return shipping, a $1 eco fee, and a 15% restocking fee (up to $50) on opened items." },
  "url": "https://example.com/returns",
  "eligibility": { "type": "window", "duration": "P30D", "anchor": "delivered" },
  "supported_resolutions": ["original_payment_method", "exchange"],
  "methods": ["in_store", "by_mail"],
  "fees": [
    { "type": "dev.ucp.shopping.fee.restocking", "basis_points": 1500, "max_amount": 5000,
      "display_text": "15% restocking fee on opened items" },
    { "methods": ["in_store"], "amount": 0 },
    { "type": "dev.ucp.shopping.fee.return_shipping", "methods": ["by_mail"], "amount": 500 },
    { "type": "com.example.fee.eco", "methods": ["by_mail"], "amount": 100, "display_text": "Eco packaging fee" }
  ]
}
```

On the order, once the jacket on line 0 has been delivered, the business adds the resolved deadline:

```json
"applies_to": ["$.line_items[0]"],
"eligibility": { "type": "window", "duration": "P30D", "anchor": "delivered", "expires_at": "2026-04-01T18:00:00Z" }
```

Resolved per channel:

- **In store:** free; the untyped `amount: 0` entry states that no fee of any kind applies.
- **By mail:** up to 15% restocking, at most $50 per unit; $5 return shipping; $1 eco fee.
- **Return deadline:** a platform shows "Return by Apr 1" on the order, and "30 days from delivery" before delivery.

## Explicit eligibility

An omitted `window` meant two opposite things, "returns at any time" and "the business did not say". `final_sale` was a boolean next to it that could contradict it. 

Google Merchant (`NUMBER_OF_DAYS_AFTER_DELIVERY`, `NO_RETURNS`, `LIFETIME_RETURNS`) and schema.org (`MerchantReturnFiniteReturnWindow`, `MerchantReturnNotPermitted`, `MerchantReturnUnlimitedWindow`) both model these states explicitly. Here they map one-to-one.

`not_accepted` states the business's own return policy, not the absence of any remedy: remedies under applicable law or a marketplace guarantee are outside this spec. A business SHOULD localize its terms to the buyer where it can, using the request context or a shipping address, so an EU buyer, for example, sees the window that applies to them.

The type is open: an unknown kind supports no inference in either direction. From 6c7ed01f, the rule that an omission never reads as unlimited is kept. Its advice to state a finite window for returns with no time limit is dropped, because `unlimited` now says that directly.

## Business-stated deadlines

The first iteration of this stack tried to make "30 days from delivery" computable by platforms. That meant mapping each anchor to an Order event and defining the day. It quickly unravelled:

- Order has no placement timestamp and no events for pickup or digital fulfillment.
- Deliveries split by quantity.
- Every platform would have needed rules for days, time zones, and missing events.

Even then, platforms would only have produced a guess at a number the business already knows. So the business states the deadline, the same way it states totals: the platform presents what the business asserts instead of recomputing it.

- **Before the anchor event,** a window is terms to present, `duration` plus `anchor`, and a platform never presents a date it computed from them.
- **Once the deadline is resolvable,** typically on the order, the business states `expires_at`. That instant carries its own offset, so no time-zone or calendar rules are needed.
- **Split deliveries:** `expires_at` is the earliest deadline.

Because nobody computes from `duration`, it can be an ISO 8601 duration in any unit:

- `P30D`: 30 days.
- `PT30M`: 30 minutes, as for perishables.
- `P1M`: one month.

Components must be greater than zero, because `not_accepted`, not a zero window, says "no returns".

Anchors collapse to three milestones: `purchased`, `fulfilled`, and `delivered`. `shipped` folds into `fulfilled`, which for a shipment is the handoff to a carrier, so the anchor list does not grow with every new fulfillment method. If its clock starts at an event no well-known anchor names, such as the earlier of actual and estimated delivery, a business MAY use its own anchor value or an earlier well-known one such as `purchased`. The window is still a guaranteed floor, met by a return requested by `expires_at`.

## Extensible, typed fees

The current shape has two fee homes with two shapes: one restocking fee on the policy and one fee per return method. A channel cannot carry two charges, such as return shipping plus an eco fee. Restocking cannot be waived in store. Every new kind, such as handling (raised by the Shopify team), needs a new field.

`fees[]` borrows two existing UCP patterns:

- **Totals-style entries.** Each entry is a typed line: `type` names what the fee is for, and an unknown vendor kind such as `com.example.fee.eco` only needs `display_text`. This is the same rule totals use to render lines they don't understand.
- **Policy-style scoping.** An entry that lists `methods` applies only to those channels. When more than one entry applies to a fee on a channel, an entry that lists the channel takes precedence over one that does not, and an entry with a `type` takes precedence over one without, the same most-specific-wins idea `policies[]` already uses.

Well-known kinds use reverse-domain names, as consent purposes do. Each has a defined unit:

- `dev.ucp.shopping.fee.restocking`: charged per returned unit.
- `dev.ucp.shopping.fee.return_shipping`: charged per shipment.
- `dev.ucp.shopping.fee.handling`: charged per return.

The price is read from which fields are present, so `type` has no second discriminator competing with it:

| Fields present | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `amount` | A flat charge; `0` means nothing is charged. |
| `basis_points` | A percentage. Exact, so 12.5% is `1250`, with no floats. `max_amount` can cap it. |
| neither | The buyer pays the actual cost, with no maximum stated. |

An entry without `type` must be `amount: 0` and states that no fee of any kind is charged where it applies, including vendor kinds and kinds defined later. `{ "amount": 0 }` alone is free returns; add a typed entry to keep one fee.

Each state has exactly one encoding, and amounts take the currency of the items the policy covers. Absence never means free. A platform may present a channel as free only when an untyped `amount: 0` entry covers it and no typed entry resolves to a charge there.

Fees are **estimated maximums**, not binding caps. The charge for a particular return depends on the item's condition, carrier rates, taxes, and how order discounts are refunded, and none of that is knowable when a policy is stated before purchase. The fee a policy states is still a term: a business MUST NOT state an `amount`, `basis_points`, or `max_amount` lower than its policy charges, and a fee it cannot bound omits them. A platform MUST NOT present a fee as the final charge. This follows the EU Consumer Rights Directive, whose model withdrawal instructions read "The cost is estimated at a maximum of approximately …" when the cost "cannot reasonably be calculated in advance".

## Design + assumptions... 

- **One governing policy per item.** Core precedence still applies: one return policy governs each item. Variations live inside that policy rather than in competing policies.
- **`description` carries what the fields don't.** Channel instructions ("print the label, drop at any UPS"), eligibility conditions ("unopened", "tags attached", "photo required"), and promotional terms such as bonus store credit go in `description`. The structured fields state only what a platform can act on.
- **Required conditions are eligibility requirements.** A condition the business requires of the item or return, such as unopened or tags attached, scopes the structured terms: they state the terms for returns that meet it, and `description` states the requirement and any terms for returns that don't. A choice the buyer makes, such as the resolution, is not a requirement.
- **Resolutions and methods are guaranteed per list.** Each listed resolution is available through at least one listed method, and each listed method accepts at least one listed resolution. A platform MUST NOT pair a specific resolution with a specific method unless only one of either is listed.
- **Channels are an open vocabulary.** A business can use values beyond `in_store`, `by_mail`, and `kiosk`, such as a returnless "keep it" refund.

## Future work

Each of these can be added later without breaking the shape in this PR:

- Per-channel windows ("30 days by mail, 60 in store"), as a scoped override inside `eligibility`.
- Per-channel resolutions ("exchanges in store only"), as entries scoped with `methods`, so a platform can present a specific resolution through a specific channel.
- Per-resolution fees ("restocking waived for store credit"), as a `resolutions` scope on fees that mirrors `methods`.
